title: South Korea's KOSPI Crashed Twice in a Week — India's Markets Logged a Third Straight Weekly Gain
excerpt: While circuit breakers halted trading in Seoul as Samsung and SK Hynix plummeted over 10 percent in an AI-fuelled rout, India's Nifty and Sensex quietly extended their winning streak, insulated by falling oil prices, RBI measures and a market structure that doesn't bet the house on one sector.
body:
The contrast could not have been starker. On Tuesday, South Korea's benchmark KOSPI index plunged nearly 10 percent, triggering automatic circuit breakers that halted trading twice in a single week. By Friday, it had fallen again — as much as 5.8 percent — before steadying. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the two memory-chip giants that together account for more than half the index's market value, each dropped over 10 percent at their intraday lows.

Meanwhile, roughly 5,000 kilometres to the west, India's Nifty 50 and Sensex quietly notched a third consecutive weekly gain — their longest winning streak in seven months. The Nifty rose to 24,056 and the Sensex to 77,100, supported by falling oil prices, a Reserve Bank of India that showed no appetite for rate hikes, and heavyweight banking stocks that attracted fresh buying interest.

## What Happened in Seoul

The carnage in South Korea was driven by a swift and vicious unwind of the global AI trade. The KOSPI had been the world's hottest major index in 2026, up more than 94 percent for the year before this week's rout — more than seven times the Nasdaq's gains. Retail investors had poured a record $39 billion into stock-focused ETFs, many of them leveraged, riding a semiconductor boom that turned SK Hynix and Samsung into the twin engines of a frenzied rally.

Then the music stopped. A combination of senior leadership departures at Alphabet, profit-taking in US tech names, concerns about structural inflation from Apple's price hikes, and South Korean regulatory pressure on leveraged semiconductor products combined to create what *Barron's* called a "three-front storm." The circuit breaker — a 20-minute pause triggered when the KOSPI falls 8 percent or more — activated twice in four days.

"These big moves are part of a growing trend of rising volatility in tech stocks generally," James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics, wrote. "This volatility is evidence of excessive froth and calls into question the sustainability of this rally."

## Why India Was Insulated

India's relative calm this week was not accidental. Three structural differences shielded the market from the worst of the global selloff.

**Sector diversification.** Unlike South Korea, where two chipmakers dominate the index, India's Nifty 50 is spread across financials, IT, consumer goods, energy, pharma and industrials. No single company accounts for more than 10 percent of the index's weight. When global tech sold off, Indian banks — which had received a policy boost from the RBI allowing loans against foreign-currency deposits — picked up the slack. HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank each climbed roughly 2.5 percent during the week.

**Oil tailwinds.** Brent crude fell to $72.70 a barrel, its lowest level since before the Iran war began in late February, as tankers exited the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Iran peace deal. For the world's third-largest oil importer, cheaper crude means a narrower current account deficit, lower inflation risk and better corporate margins. BofA Global Research noted in a research note that markets had begun to reduce long USD/INR positions as macro deterioration concerns faded.

**Central bank signalling.** RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra told ET Now that it was "premature to discuss rate hikes" because the central bank did not yet see signs of inflation becoming broad-based. The message — lower for longer — supports earnings multiples, consumption and bank lending, all of which are pillars of the Indian equity story.

## The Lesson for NRI Investors

The week offered a real-time case study in concentration risk. South Korea's KOSPI is, as *Barron's* put it, "the canary in the tech coal mine" — a market so dominated by semiconductors that a single sector rotation can trigger systemic stress. India's market, for all its own frothiness in small-caps and mid-caps, simply does not carry that structural vulnerability.

That does not mean India is immune to global shocks. The Nifty IT index fell more than 1 percent during the week, and foreign institutional investors sold ₹2,080 crore. But domestic institutional investors more than compensated, pumping ₹11,100 crore into equities. India's market is increasingly driven by local capital — monthly SIP inflows now exceed ₹25,000 crore — which provides a cushion that Korea's retail-leveraged, ETF-heavy market does not enjoy.

For NRI investors allocating between US-listed tech, Indian equities and other Asian markets, this week's divergence reinforces a simple principle: broad sectoral exposure and macro tailwinds matter more than riding the hottest trade. India's third weekly gain was not spectacular — the Nifty advanced just 0.2 percent. But in a week when South Korea's market triggered circuit breakers and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 7.7 percent, boring was exactly the right kind of performance.

*Sources: Reuters; Wall Street Journal; CNN; Barron's*
